# Selected exercise solutions {#sec-solutions}

These solutions illustrate reasoning and provide runnable checks. They do not replace explanations in a student's own words. Interpretations of simulated data apply only to the teaching exercise.

## Foundations and import

For Chapter 1, 11.2 kg harvested from 20 m² gives 5.6 t/ha. Dividing mass by area initially gives kg/m², so the conversion to t/ha is still required.

```{r}
11.2 / 20 * 10
numbers <- 1:30
numbers[numbers < 8]
numbers[numbers < 8 | numbers > 12]
numbers[numbers %in% c(2, 6, 12)]
m <- matrix(1:20, nrow = 4, ncol = 5)
rowMeans(m)
m[2, 3]
class(c(1, "2"))
```

The matrix fills by column unless `byrow = TRUE` is specified. The combined numeric/text vector is character. A character column cannot be averaged as though it were numeric without a validated conversion.

```{r}
crop <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv")
small <- crop[, c("plot_id", "treatment", "yield_t_ha")]
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(small, "outputs/three_columns.csv", row.names = FALSE)
reopened <- read.csv("outputs/three_columns.csv")
stopifnot(identical(names(small), names(reopened)), ncol(reopened) == 3)
```

## Cleaning and wrangling

```{r}
dirty <- read.csv("data/crop_dirty.csv")
deduplicated <- unique(dirty)
c(before = nrow(dirty), after = nrow(deduplicated))
deduplicated$treatment <- trimws(deduplicated$treatment)
deduplicated$treatment[deduplicated$treatment == "control"] <- "Control"
with(deduplicated, tapply(is.na(yield_t_ha), treatment, sum))
library(dplyr)
crop |>
  group_by(treatment, variety) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(yield_t_ha), sd = sd(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop")
```

There are 61 entry records and 60 after removal of the exact duplicate. Missingness counts are reported by treatment, not silently discarded. A conflicting duplicate requires checking identifiers, harvest dates, and source sheets before resolution.

## Graphics, description, and EDA

```{r}
soil <- read.csv("data/soil.csv")
x <- soil$available_n_mg_kg
c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), variance = var(x), sd = sd(x), IQR = IQR(x))
table(soil$soil_class)
```

Nitrogen means, medians, SDs, and IQRs have units mg/kg; variance has units (mg/kg)². An extreme positive value generally shifts the mean and SD more than the median and IQR. More observations can improve precision of a mean without reducing biological variability among individual observations. Leaves from the same treated plant are subsamples unless treatment was independently assigned at the leaf level and the analysis supports that design.

An EDA memo should identify treatment–nitrogen confounding, variation among blocks, the simulated source, and the observational unit. Numerical summaries must be taken from executed output. A pooled nitrogen–yield trend cannot separate management components that vary together.

## Growth and time series

```{r}
growth <- read.csv("data/growth.csv")
fit <- nls(biomass_g_m2 ~ A / (1 + exp(-k * (day - ti))), growth,
           start = list(A = 1000, k = .07, ti = 50))
predict(fit, data.frame(day = 75))
```

Day 75 is inside the observed 10–120 day range, so this is interpolation. It estimates a mean curve response under the model, not an exact new quadrat measurement. The logistic inflection biomass is `A/2`; the Gompertz value is `A/e`. A fit based only on early observations may not identify the plateau reliably.

For forecasting, use the first eight years as training and the last two as holdout, as in Chapter 10. Report test MAE/RMSE for both methods. Fitting on all ten years first would let future information affect model selection and estimates. A centred moving average includes future values and is not a directly available real-time predictor.

## Inference, ANOVA, and regression

```{r}
data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
fit_aov <- aov(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth)
df.residual(fit_aov)
TukeyHSD(fit_aov)
```

The one-way global null is equality of the three population group means. There are 27 residual degrees of freedom. A Tukey interval excluding zero indicates evidence of a difference for that pair under the simultaneous procedure and its assumptions. A p-value of 0.08 is not proof of no effect; the effect estimate and interval show which magnitudes remain compatible with the data.

The paired soil test matches the same plots before and after. An unpaired analysis discards that pairing. The pest table has independent plot statuses as its units; expected counts must be inspected before trusting a chi-square approximation.

In regression, a rainfall coefficient is a conditional change in predicted mean yield per millimetre, holding nitrogen fixed. A prediction interval is wider than a confidence interval because it also represents individual-outcome variation. A random row split is inappropriate when observations from the same farm, future period, or nearby spatial cluster would leak information across training and test sets.

## Field experimental designs

```{r}
rb <- read.csv("data/rcbd_varieties.csv")
rb$block <- factor(rb$block); rb$variety <- factor(rb$variety)
with_block <- anova(aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + variety, data = rb))
without_block <- anova(aov(yield_t_ha ~ variety, data = rb))
c(error_ms_rcbd = with_block["Residuals", "Mean Sq"],
  error_ms_ignoring_blocks = without_block["Residuals", "Mean Sq"])
```

Ignoring blocks moves block variation into the error, so the error mean square rises from about 0.039 to 0.116 and the CD widens. The relative efficiency of about 2.6 says a CRD would need about 2.6 times as many replicates for the same precision. Blocks stay in the model in any case, because they were part of the randomization.

In the Latin square, error degrees of freedom are $(t-1)(t-2) = 4 \times 3 = 12$: from 24 total degrees of freedom, rows, columns, and treatments each use 4.

In the split-plot, the wrong one-error analysis tests irrigation against a pooled error that is too small for main plots and too large for subplots. Its irrigation F-value is inflated, and the irrigation-by-nitrogen interaction, significant with error (b), becomes non-significant. The correct conclusions are those from the analysis with `Error(block / irrigation)`.

## Tests for proportions and ratios

For 212 of 250 seeds, `prop.test(212, 250, p = 0.85)` estimates 84.8% germination; the interval includes 85%, so the sample is consistent with the standard. For 152 purple and 48 white, `chisq.test(c(152, 48), p = c(3, 1) / 4)` gives expected counts 150 and 50 and a small chi-square statistic (about 0.11 on 1 df), consistent with a 3:1 ratio.

## AI-assisted analysis

A prompt without the design usually produces `aov(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen * variety)` with no block term, or with `block` left numeric (1 df instead of 3). Both run. The design check is the degrees of freedom: for 4 blocks, 3 nitrogen levels, and 2 varieties, expect 3, 2, 1, 2, and 15 for block, nitrogen, variety, interaction, and error. A known-answer test for a CD function can use the toy data with error mean square 1, $r = 3$, and 6 error df: CD = `qt(0.975, 6) * sqrt(2 / 3)`, about 2.00.

## Reporting and project evaluation

`echo: false` executes code but hides the code listing; `eval: false` does not execute it. A complete project includes data provenance, raw inputs, cleaning code, analysis source, environment information, and rendered output. Interpretive exercises should be marked for the connection between question, design, method, uncertainty, and limitations rather than agreement with a preferred p-value.

## STAT 531 modules

```{r sol-setup}
#| include: false
options(digits = 4, scipen = 6)
```

### Exploratory analysis and distributions (@sec-met-eda, @sec-distributions)

For the yacon data, dry root matter differs strongly between localities; Lima has the lowest means at every fertiliser dose.

```{r sol-met}
library(agricolae)
data(yacon)
round(with(yacon, tapply(roots, list(locality, dose), mean)), 2)
```

The pesticide and weed probabilities follow from the binomial and Poisson functions. For spray C the counts have variance close to the mean (a Poisson fit is reasonable), but pooled over all sprays the variance is more than five times the mean: mixing sprays with different means produces over-dispersion.

```{r sol-dist}
c(P_X_eq_10 = dbinom(10, 15, 0.7), P_X_le_8 = pbinom(8, 15, 0.7),
  P_no_weeds = dpois(0, 2.5))
spray_c <- InsectSprays$count[InsectSprays$spray == "C"]
c(mean_C = mean(spray_c), var_C = var(spray_c),
  mean_all = mean(InsectSprays$count), var_all = var(InsectSprays$count))
```

### Tests of significance (@sec-large-sample, @sec-small-sample)

```{r sol-tests}
data(plrv)
hyo <- plrv$Yield[plrv$Locality == "Hyo-02"]
z <- (mean(hyo) - 40) / (sd(hyo) / sqrt(length(hyo)))
c(mean = mean(hyo), z = z, p_one_sided = pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE))
prop.test(248, 400, p = 0.55, alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)$p.value
prop.test(c(72, 54), c(150, 150), alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)$p.value
chisq.test(c(290, 110), p = c(3, 1) / 4)
```

Mean yield at Huancayo (45.7 t/ha) significantly exceeds 40 t/ha. The adoption rate is significantly greater than 55%, and the new trap is significantly more effective at the 5% level. The tall:dwarf counts agree with a 3:1 ratio.

For the `sleep` data the same patients received both drugs, so the paired test is correct:

```{r sol-sleep}
with(sleep, t.test(extra[group == 1], extra[group == 2], paired = TRUE))
```

### Analysis of variance (@sec-anova-crd, @sec-research-designs, @sec-contrasts)

```{r sol-anova}
pg_fit <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(pg_fit)
library(emmeans)
contrast(emmeans(pg_fit, ~ group), method = "trt.vs.ctrl")
HSD.test(aov(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts), "feed")$groups
```

The `PlantGrowth` treatments differ ($p = 0.016$), but neither treatment differs significantly from the control by Dunnett's test: the significant F comes from the difference between the two treatments. The orthogonal contrasts confirm this:

```{r sol-contrast}
pg <- PlantGrowth
contrasts(pg$group) <- cbind(ctrl_vs_trt = c(2, -1, -1), t1_vs_t2 = c(0, 1, -1))
summary(aov(weight ~ group, data = pg),
        split = list(group = list("Control vs treatments" = 1, "Trt 1 vs trt 2" = 2)))
```

The CD at 1% for the sweet potato experiment is

```{r sol-cd1}
qt(0.995, 8) * sqrt(2 * 22.489 / 3)
```

For the `npk` experiment, nitrogen and potassium are the important factors:

```{r sol-npk}
summary(aov(yield ~ block + N * P * K, data = npk))
```

### Covariance and mixed models (@sec-ancova, @sec-mixed-models)

```{r sol-ancova}
library(agridat)
apple_fit <- aov(yield ~ block + prev + trt, data = pearce.apple)
pairs(emmeans(apple_fit, ~ trt))
```

Only treatment E and the standard practice S differ significantly after Tukey adjustment.

```{r sol-mixed}
hyo2 <- droplevels(subset(plrv, Locality == "Hyo-02"))
hyo2$Rep <- factor(hyo2$Rep)
tab <- summary(aov(Yield ~ Rep + Genotype, data = hyo2))[[1]]
s2g <- (tab[2, "Mean Sq"] - tab[3, "Mean Sq"]) / 3
s2e <- tab[3, "Mean Sq"]
c(sigma2_g = s2g, sigma2_e = s2e, H2_mean = s2g / (s2g + s2e / 3))
```

Genotypic variance at Huancayo is large relative to error, giving a high entry-mean heritability (about 0.93).

### Regression and multivariate methods (@sec-multiple-regression to @sec-discriminant)

```{r sol-reg}
cor.test(~ Height + Girth, data = trees)$p.value
summary(lm(Volume ~ Girth + I(Girth^2), data = trees))$coefficients
fit3 <- lm(log(Volume) ~ log(Girth) + log(Height), data = trees)
exp(predict(fit3, data.frame(Girth = 15, Height = 80), interval = "prediction"))
```

Height and diameter are significantly correlated; the quadratic term is significant; a tree 15 inches in diameter and 80 ft tall is predicted to contain about 38 cubic feet (95% prediction interval 32 to 45).

```{r sol-multi}
round(prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)$rotation[, 1], 2)
factanal(factors = 2, covmat = ability.cov)$loadings
library(MASS)
mean(qda(Species ~ ., data = iris, CV = TRUE)$class == iris$Species)
```

PC1 of `iris` is dominated by petal length, petal width and sepal length. In the ability tests, reading and vocabulary load on one factor (verbal ability) and blocks, picture and maze on the other (spatial ability). QDA classifies slightly less accurately than LDA (97.3% against 98% cross-validated).

### Non-linear models (@sec-nonlinear)

```{r sol-nl}
coef(nls(rate ~ SSmicmen(conc, Vm, K), data = subset(Puromycin, state == "treated")))
coef(nls(height ~ SSasymp(age, Asym, R0, lrc), data = subset(Loblolly, Seed == "301")))
```

The treated enzyme reaches a maximum velocity of about 213 counts/min², with half-saturation at 0.064 ppm; tree 301 approaches an asymptotic height of about 96 ft.
